paragraphs: The gentleman of leisure is a rich man who does not need to work. He lives in a time that is almost peaceful. He uses more food and other things than he needs to live and stay strong. He also chooses the quality of the things he uses. He takes a lot, and he takes the best. This is true for food, drink, drugs, houses, servants, jewels, clothes, weapons, games, lucky objects, and even gods. Over time, these things become better. The main reason for this is surely comfort. But comfort does not stay the only reason. There is also a rule about honour, or a good name. This rule chooses which new things stay. When a man uses these better things, it shows that he is rich. So using them brings honour. The opposite is also true. Some men do not use enough good things, or things of good quality. People think that these men are lower and worse than others.

So the gentleman starts to see very small differences in the quality of food, drink and other things. This changes his way of life, his education and the way he uses his mind. He is no longer only a strong, brave fighting man who wins. He must now also train his taste. Without good taste, he will look stupid. He must know quite exactly which things are noble and which things are low. He becomes an expert. He knows about good food of different kinds, drinks for men, and small pretty objects. He knows about the right clothes and buildings, and about weapons, games, dancers and drugs. Learning about taste takes time and work. So his free life slowly becomes hard work. He must work to learn how to live a life of leisure in the right way, so that everyone can see it. There is a second rule. He must use a lot of the right things. He must also know how to use them correctly. This is where good manners come from, as an earlier chapter of the book explains. The fine manners of the upper class follow one rule. Veblen calls it conspicuous leisure and conspicuous consumption. Conspicuous means easy to see. People must see that you do not work, and they must see that you spend.

For the gentleman of leisure, using expensive things in front of others brings him a good name. But his money grows, and soon he cannot show all his wealth alone in this way. So he asks friends and rivals to help him. He gives them expensive presents, big dinners and parties. Presents and dinners probably started for a different reason, not only to show off. But very early, people used them for this. Today, this is the main reason for these customs. Some costly parties are very good for this, for example the potlatch, a great feast with many gifts, or the ball, a big dance. The host wants to compare himself with a rival. The rival eats and drinks the host's good things for him. At the same time, the rival sees that the host has too many good things to use alone. He also sees that the host knows the rules of good manners very well.
